lead.t: Infection is a risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma
lead.s: Internal Medicine CAT 1 (MBChB 4), 2022: liver, pancreas and bone marrow, 30 MCQ

b: Epidemiology: commonest primary liver cancer; male to female about 3-8 : 1 ; very common in sub-Saharan Africa and East Asia.

Risk factors: chronic hepatitis B (about 200-fold risk, and HBV can cause HCC even without cirrhosis) , hepatitis C, cirrhosis of any cause , alcohol , aflatoxin B1 (contaminated maize and groundnuts; the p53 codon 249 mutation), NAFLD/NASH
Pathogenesis: repeated injury and regeneration, viral DNA integration and aflatoxin-induced mutations cause dysplastic nodules, then carcinoma. Vascular invasion (portal vein) is common.

Presentation: weight loss, right upper quadrant pain or mass, decompensation of known cirrhosis (new ascites, jaundice, encephalopathy), paraneoplastic features (hypoglycaemia, polycythaemia, hypercalcaemia), rupture with haemoperitoneum.
Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) raised; above 1000 ng/mL is highly suggestive (it can be normal in some HCCs and raised in other conditions).

qs.q: A 40-year-old man with chronic hepatitis C is treated with direct-acting antivirals. After 12 weeks, his HCV RNA is undetectable. Why is he still at risk for hepatocellular carcinoma?
o: Persistent low-level viral replication in extrahepatic sites
Latent viral infection in hepatocytes that can reactivate
Accumulated liver damage and fibrosis from prior inflammation
Ongoing immune activation causing chronic systemic inflammation
Viral integration into the host genome leading to transformation
qs.e: HCV does not integrate into the host genome; cancer risk persists due to pre-existing fibrosis and chronic inflammation.

qs.q: A public health agency investigates an outbreak of acute hepatic necrosis and subsequent hepatocellular carcinoma linked to contaminated peanut imports. Chemical analysis identifies aflatoxin B1. Which genus of fungi produces this potent mycotoxin?
o: Penicillium species growing on ripening cheeses in subterranean cellars
Aspergillus species contaminating stored cereal grains under humid conditions
Fusarium species invading corn stalks during wet seasonal agricultural periods
Claviceps species parasitizing rye heads in temperate grain crop fields
Stachybotrys species colonizing damp indoor cellulose building material surfaces
qs.e: Aspergillus flavus and Aspergillus parasiticus produce aflatoxins in improperly stored crops like peanuts and corn.

qs.q: Which tumor marker combination demonstrates the highest utility for the early detection and surveillance of Hepatocellular Carcinoma?
o: Cancer antigen and Human epididymis protein four
qs.e: The combined measurement of Des-gamma-carboxyprothrombin (DCP/PIVKA-II) and Alpha-fetoprotein improves sensitivity for early detection of hepatocellular carcinoma. CEA and CA 19-9 are gastrointestinal markers rather than hepatocellular ones.

qs.q: Which chemical carcinogen derived from a fungus contaminating poorly stored grain foods most commonly induces hepatocellular carcinoma?
qs.e: Aflatoxin B1 from Aspergillus growing on poorly stored grains causes liver cancer. Phorbol esters act as promoters rather than direct hepatotoxins.

qs.q: A 62-year-old man with chronic hepatitis B develops hepatocellular carcinoma with inactivation of the p53 gene. Which of the following is the normal cellular function of p53?
o: Induction of local angiogenesis through VEGF secretion
Induction of apoptosis in cells with irreparable DNA damage
Direct repair of DNA double-strand breaks
Phosphorylation of RB to permit cell cycle progression
qs.e: p53 normally halts the cell cycle for DNA repair; if damage is unfixable, it triggers apoptosis. Losing p53 allows genetically damaged cells to survive and accumulate further mutations.

qs.q: A patient diagnosed with metastatic hepatocellular carcinoma is monitored during treatment. Which serum tumour marker is classically associated with this malignancy and germ cell tumours?
qs.e: Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) is a classic serum tumour marker elevated in hepatocellular carcinoma and germ cell tumours. Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) is typically associated with colorectal and gastric cancers.

qs.q: A 45-year-old patient presents with hepatocellular carcinoma linked to a chronic viral infection. Besides chronic inflammation, what specific mechanism is implicated in oncogenesis by Hepatitis B virus?
o: Production of the Tax transforming protein
Insertional mutagenesis into the host genome
Direct alteration of the tumor microenvironment
qs.e: Hepatitis B contributes to hepatocellular carcinoma through chronic inflammation combined with insertional mutagenesis into the host genome. The Tax protein is associated with HTLV-1, not Hepatitis B.

qs.q: A patient with chronic HBV develops hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Which of the following statements best describes the relationship between liver pathology and HCC risk in these patients?
o: Cirrhosis is an absolute prerequisite for malignant transformation.
HCC only develops after macroscopic cirrhosis is established.
The carcinoma risk is independent of the presence of cirrhosis.
HCC occurs exclusively in patients with HBV genotype A.
qs.e: Chronic HBV infection is associated with chronic liver disease and HCC, but the carcinoma risk is independent of the presence of cirrhosis. Cirrhosis and HCC are complications seen with chronic infection, yet neither strictly depends on the other to manifest.

es.q: Compare Hepatitis B (HBV) and Hepatitis C (HCV) regarding their rates of chronicity in adults and their respective associations with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).
es.m: HBV leads to chronicity in 5-10% of infected adults, whereas HCV chronic infection occurs in approximately 85% of cases. Both HBV (via the HBx protein) and HCV are significant risk factors for the development of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).
es.s: Liver Histology, Physiology and Pathology — Practice Questions

es.q: A 28-year-old male presents to the emergency department with symptoms concerning for acute viral hepatitis. His serological markers indicate HBsAg negative, Anti-HBs negative, and Anti-HBc IgM positive. 1. Interpret these serological findings. What specific phase of HBV infection do they represent?
es.m: 1. These serological findings represent the **'window period'** of acute HBV infection. During this phase, HBsAg has disappeared, and Anti-HBs antibodies have not yet fully developed, leaving Anti-HBc IgM as the sole marker of acute infection. 2. A positive HBeAg indicates **high infectivity and active viral replication**. 3. Both **chronic HBV** and **chronic HCV** infections are significant risk factors for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).

Chronic HBV infection carries a significant risk of progressing to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) due to the HBx protein and chronic inflammation. * **Hepatitis C Virus (HCV):** An RNA virus, predominantly transmitted parenterally (e.g., IV drug use, contaminated blood products). A high percentage, about 85%, of individuals infected with HCV will develop chronic hepatitis. Chronic HC

es.q: List the major risk factors associated with Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC) and identify a key laboratory marker highly suggestive of this malignancy.
es.m: Major risk factors for Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC) include: 1. Hepatitis B Virus (HBV) infection (1 mark) 2. Hepatitis C Virus (HCV) infection (1 mark) 3. Chronic alcohol use (1 mark) 4. Aflatoxin B1 exposure (1 mark) 5. Cirrhosis from any cause (1 mark) A key laboratory marker highly suggestive of HCC is Alpha-Fetoprotein (AFP) > 1000 ng/ml (1 mark).

ai.summary: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the most common primary liver cancer, often arising in the context of chronic liver disease and cirrhosis. Diagnosis relies on imaging and alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) levels, with staging guiding treatment decisions. Management focuses on curative or palliative options depending on disease extent.

sections.p: Hepatocellular carcinoma is a malignant tumor originating from hepatocytes, the main cells of the liver. It is a major cause of cancer-related death worldwide, particularly in regions with high rates of chronic viral hepatitis.
b: Often develops in patients with underlying chronic liver disease, especially cirrhosis from any cause.
Diagnosis is typically made using imaging (ultrasound, CT, MRI) and elevated alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) levels.

t.b: Detects liver lesions and assesses their characteristics.
A tumor marker that can be elevated in HCC.

sections.p: HCC staging systems, like the Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer (BCLC) staging system, integrate tumor burden, liver function, and patient performance status to guide treatment and predict prognosis.
b: Early-stage HCC is often asymptomatic and amenable to curative treatments.
Advanced-stage HCC is associated with poor prognosis and requires palliative management.

sections.p: Chronic viral hepatitis B and C are the leading causes globally. Other significant risk factors include alcohol-related cirrhosis, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), and certain inherited metabolic disorders.
b: Chronic Hepatitis B infection
Chronic Hepatitis C infection
Alcoholic liver disease (cirrhosis)
Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD)/Non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH)
Cirrhosis from any cause (e.g., autoimmune hepatitis, hemochromatosis, Wilson's disease)
Aflatoxin exposure (from moldy food, common in some tropical regions)

sections.p: Early HCC is often asymptomatic and detected during screening for chronic liver disease. As it progresses, patients may develop symptoms related to liver dysfunction or the tumor itself.
b: Abdominal pain or discomfort, especially in the upper right quadrant.
Unexplained weight loss.
Fatigue and weakness.
Jaundice (yellowing of skin and eyes).
Abdominal swelling (ascites).
Nausea and vomiting.

sections.p: Diagnostic workup aims to confirm the presence of HCC, assess its extent, and evaluate the underlying liver function.

t.b: Assesses the degree of liver damage and dysfunction.
Checks for anemia, thrombocytopenia, or leukocytosis.
Evaluates the liver's synthetic function and clotting ability.
Identifies chronic hepatitis B or C infection as a cause.
Primary screening tool for HCC in at-risk individuals.
Provides detailed imaging of liver lesions and vascularity.
Tumor marker for HCC.

sections.p: Complications arise from tumor progression, liver failure, or treatment side effects. Urgent medical attention is needed for signs of decompensated cirrhosis or tumor rupture.
b: Gastrointestinal bleeding (from varices or tumor erosion).
Hepatic encephalopathy (confusion due to liver failure).
Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP).
Ascites refractory to diuretics.
Tumor rupture with hemoperitoneum.
Acute liver failure.

sections.p: Treatment strategies are tailored to the stage of HCC, liver function, and patient's overall health, aiming for cure, local control, or palliation.
b: Curative options (for early-stage HCC): Surgical resection, liver transplantation, or ablation (e.g., radiofrequency ablation).
Loco-regional therapies (for intermediate-stage HCC): Transarterial chemoembolization (TACE) or radioembolization (TARE) to control tumor growth.
Systemic therapy (for advanced-stage HCC): Targeted therapies (e.g., sorafenib, lenvatinib) or immunotherapy to slow disease progression.
Supportive care: Management of ascites, encephalopathy, and nutritional support.

sections.p: Regular surveillance is crucial for early detection in at-risk populations. Prevention strategies focus on managing underlying liver disease and avoiding risk factors.
b: Screening with ultrasound and AFP every 6 months for patients with cirrhosis or chronic hepatitis B.
Hepatitis B vaccination to prevent primary infection.
Antiviral therapy for chronic hepatitis B and C to reduce liver inflammation and fibrosis.
Limiting alcohol consumption.
Weight management and healthy diet to prevent/manage NAFLD.
Avoiding exposure to aflatoxins.

sections.p: Other liver lesions or conditions can mimic HCC, requiring careful differentiation.
b: Benign liver tumors (e.g., hemangioma, focal nodular hyperplasia).
Liver metastases from other primary cancers.
Cholangiocarcinoma (bile duct cancer).
Abscesses or granulomas.

sections.p: Certain findings can be misleading, necessitating a comprehensive clinical assessment.
b: Normal AFP levels can occur in patients with confirmed HCC.
Elevated AFP can be seen in non-cancerous liver conditions (e.g., active hepatitis, cirrhosis).
Imaging findings can be equivocal, especially for small lesions or in the presence of severe fatty liver or cirrhosis.
Patients with chronic liver disease may have baseline abnormalities in LFTs that can mask or be confused with changes due to HCC.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden onset of severe abdominal pain.
Vomiting blood or passing black, tarry stools.

faq.q: What is the main risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma?
faq.a: Chronic infection with Hepatitis B or C virus, leading to cirrhosis, is the most significant risk factor globally.
Yes, early-stage HCC can be cured with treatments like surgery, liver transplant, or ablation, especially if detected during screening.
Yes, regular screening with ultrasound and AFP for individuals at high risk (e.g., those with cirrhosis) is crucial for early detection and better outcomes.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: A focused history and systematic physical exam reveal clues to underlying chronic liver disease, tumour burden and complications, guiding further work‑up and urgency of referral.
b: Duration and aetiology of liver disease (HBV, HCV, alcohol, NAFLD, aflatoxin exposure).
Prior antiviral or antiviral‑related therapy and sustained virologic response.
Symptoms of early HCC (new right‑upper‑quadrant discomfort, weight loss, early satiety).
Signs of decompensation (ascites, encephalopathy, variceal bleed, jaundice).
Risk modifiers: HIV co‑infection, diabetes, obesity, family history of HCC.
Medication and herbal use (steroids, herbal hepatotoxins).
Social history (occupational exposure to aflatoxin, alcohol quantity).
Vaccination status for HBV and hepatitis A.

t.a: Inspection for jaundice, spider naevi, palmar erythema, cachexia
t.b: Detect chronic liver disease stigmata; positive indicates portal hypertension or synthetic dysfunction; cannot quantify severity.

t.a: Palpation for liver edge, tenderness, hepatomegaly
t.b: Enlarged, firm liver suggests tumour or cirrhosis; cannot differentiate benign from malignant.

t.a: Percussion for liver span and shifting dullness
t.b: Detect ascites; shifting dullness positive when fluid moves to dependent flank on position change; cannot estimate volume precisely.
Positive when a wave is felt across abdomen indicating moderate‑to‑large ascites; cannot detect small fluid collections.
Bruit suggests arterialised tumour blood flow; positive supports HCC but not diagnostic.

t.a: Neurological exam for asterixis and West‑Haven grade
t.b: Identifies hepatic encephalopathy; grade predicts severity; does not locate tumour.

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Select investigations answer specific clinical questions; when a test is unavailable, use the next best alternative and interpret within the local resource context.
b: Ultrasound with Doppler – first‑line imaging for focal lesion, vascular invasion, portal vein thrombosis; typical HCC shows arterial hyper‑enhancement and rapid wash‑out.
Triphasic CT or MRI – confirmatory imaging; arterial phase hyper‑enhancement plus wash‑out in portal/delayed phase is diagnostic without biopsy.
Serum AFP – supportive marker; >400 ng/mL strongly suggests HCC but normal AFP does not exclude it.
Liver function panel – bilirubin, albumin, INR; used for Child‑Pugh scoring.
Complete blood count – thrombocytopenia may indicate portal hypertension.
Serum‑ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) – calculate (ascitic albumin – serum albumin); ≥1.1 g/dL indicates portal hypertension‑related ascites, guiding management.
Viral serologies – HBsAg, anti‑HBc IgG, HCV RNA; confirm chronic infection and need for antiviral therapy.
Renal function – creatinine, electrolytes; assess eligibility for systemic therapy.

t.b: Does a focal lesion exist? Positive for hypoechoic mass; if arterial flow on Doppler, raises suspicion for HCC.
Confirms imaging criteria for HCC; arterial hyper‑enhancement + wash‑out = diagnostic; also assesses tumour size and extra‑hepatic spread.
Is tumour marker elevated? >400 ng/mL strongly supports HCC; normal does not rule out early disease.
What is liver functional reserve? Points from bilirubin, albumin, INR, ascites, encephalopathy; class A‑C guides treatment options.
Is ascites due to portal hypertension? SAAG ≥ 1.1 g/dL indicates portal hypertension; lower suggests peritoneal disease or infection.

t.a: MRI with liver‑specific contrast (if CT unavailable)
t.b: Provides same diagnostic criteria; useful when iodinated contrast contraindicated.
When imaging is inconclusive; histology confirms HCC but carries bleeding risk; avoid if typical imaging already diagnostic.

sections.p: Diagnosis rests on imaging criteria or histology plus assessment of liver function; staging integrates tumour burden, performance status and hepatic reserve.
b: Diagnosis of HCC: arterial phase hyper‑enhancement with wash‑out on CT/MRI OR lesion ≥2 cm with typical imaging pattern; biopsy only if atypical.
BCLC stage 0: single ≤2 cm, Child‑Pugh A, ECOG 0 – curative options (resection, ablation).
BCLC stage A: single ≤5 cm or up to 3 lesions ≤3 cm, Child‑Pugh A‑B, ECOG 0‑1 – resection, transplant, or ablation.
BCLC stage B: multinodular, preserved liver function, ECOG 0‑1 – trans‑arterial chemo‑embolisation (TACE).
BCLC stage C: vascular invasion or extra‑hepatic spread, any Child‑Pugh, ECOG 1‑2 – systemic therapy (atezolizumab + bevacizumab or alternatives).
BCLC stage D: decompensated cirrhosis, ECOG ≥ 3 – best supportive care.
Milan criteria for transplant: single ≤5 cm or up to 3 lesions ≤3 cm, no macrovascular invasion – guides listing for liver transplantation.

sections.p: Several hepatic lesions mimic HCC on imaging; careful clinical correlation and targeted tests separate them.

t.b: Often presents with larger mass, delayed central enhancement; CA‑19‑9 elevated; differentiate by lack of arterial wash‑out and biliary dilation.
Central scar with delayed enhancement; normal AFP; iso‑intense on hepatobiliary phase MRI; benign, no portal vein invasion.
Iso‑ or hypoechoic on US, no arterial hyper‑enhancement; stable size on serial imaging; AFP normal.
Multiple peripheral lesions, often rim‑enhancing; primary tumour history; AFP usually normal; biopsy if uncertain.

sections.p: A structured ladder guides clinicians from stabilisation to curative or palliative therapy, with clear triggers for escalation or referral.
b: 1. Stabilise: control pain, correct coagulopathy, treat ascites/encephalopathy, ensure haemodynamic stability.
2. Assess resectability: imaging (triphasic CT/MRI), liver function (Child‑Pugh, ALBI), performance status (ECOG).

3. Curative options: (a) Surgical resection for solitary lesions, Child‑Pugh A‑B, adequate FLR; (b) Percutaneous ablation (radiofrequency or microwave) for ≤3 cm lesions; (c) Liver transplantation for BCLC 0‑A within Milan criteria.
4. Bridge to transplant or down‑stage: trans‑arterial chemo‑embolisation (TACE) for intermediate disease, or selective radiotherapy (Y‑90) when TACE contraindicated.
5. First‑line systemic therapy for advanced disease: atezolizumab + bevacizumab where available; alternative: sorafenib or lenvatinib if anti‑VEGF contraindicated.
6. Monitor response: imaging every 8‑12 weeks, AFP trend, liver function, and adverse‑event checklists.
7. Escalate: progression on TACE → consider systemic therapy; refractory ascites or encephalopathy → refer to transplant centre or palliative care.
8. Palliative care: symptom control, analgesia, nutritional support, and enrolment in clinical trials when possible.

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Key toxicities of the main therapies and practical steps to mitigate them.
b: Bevacizumab: hypertension, proteinuria, bleeding, GI perforation – monitor BP weekly, hold for grade ≥3 proteinuria, avoid in recent variceal bleed or uncontrolled coagulopathy.
Sorafenib/lenvatinib: hand‑foot skin reaction, diarrhoea, hypertension, hepatic decompensation – dose‑reduce or stop for grade ≥3 toxicity; treat skin reaction with emollients and topical steroids.
TACE (doxorubicin‑laden beads): post‑embolisation syndrome (fever, pain, LFT rise) – give analgesia, antipyretics, monitor LFTs; avoid in Child‑Pugh C.
Radiofrequency ablation: thermal injury to bile ducts, bleeding – use ultrasound guidance, stop if pain or temperature rise suggests ductal injury.

sections.p: Recognise life‑threatening events early and act promptly.
b: Acute variceal bleed: massive haematemesis, hypotension – immediate resuscitation, octreotide infusion, urgent endoscopy; refer to gastro‑enterology for band ligation.
Hepatorenal syndrome: rising creatinine, oliguria, no shock – start albumin 1 g/kg day 1 then 20‑40 g/day, consider terlipressin; early transplant referral.

Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis: fever, abdominal pain, new encephalopathy, SAAG > 1.1 g/dL, PMN ≥ 250 cells/µL – start cefotaxime or ceftriaxone, albumin 1.5 g/kg day 1 then 1 g/kg day 3; ICU if shock.
Tumour rupture with hemoperitoneum: sudden abdominal distension, shock – emergent resuscitation, consider urgent TACE or surgery; transfer to tertiary centre.
Severe immune‑related hepatitis (ALT > 5 × ULN) on checkpoint inhibitors – hold therapy, start high‑dose steroids, consider mycophenolate if no response.

sections.p: Co‑morbidities that modify presentation, investigations, and therapy.
b: HIV co‑infection: faster progression, lower CD4 may increase infection risk; check CD4, viral load, avoid drug interactions with protease inhibitors (e.g., sorafenib metabolism).
Active tuberculosis: hepatotoxic anti‑TB drugs can worsen liver function; prioritize TB treatment, consider non‑hepatotoxic HCC options, monitor LFTs closely.
Malnutrition/micronutrient deficiency: worsens sarcopenia, impacts surgical candidacy; assess BMI, serum albumin, provide high‑protein diet and supplementation.
Pregnancy: limited imaging (avoid CT), avoid teratogenic systemic agents; consider ablation if lesion ≤3 cm and gestation <20 weeks, otherwise defer definitive therapy.
Diabetes mellitus: higher risk of NASH‑related HCC; optimise glycaemic control, monitor for drug‑induced hypoglycaemia with sorafenib.
Alcohol use: additive hepatotoxicity, increased bleeding risk; counsel cessation, avoid drugs that raise INR, monitor for withdrawal.
Renal impairment: dose‑adjust or avoid nephrotoxic agents (e.g., contrast), prefer MRI without gadolinium if eGFR < 30 mL/min, adjust systemic therapy choice.
Age extremes: children – rare, usually transplant; elderly – frailty, higher toxicity, favour less invasive options; adjust performance‑status thresholds.

sections.p: Tailored approaches for populations with unique needs.
b: Children: HCC usually linked to metabolic disease; transplant is primary curative option; avoid TACE due to vessel size, use pediatric dosing of systemic agents.
Pregnancy: limit radiation, use ultrasound/MRI without contrast; postpone systemic therapy until postpartum; manage ascites with paracentesis, avoid teratogenic drugs.
Elderly (>70 y): assess frailty (Fried criteria), prioritize quality of life; consider ablation over resection, use lower‑intensity systemic regimens, monitor for polypharmacy interactions.
People with HIV: ensure ART adherence, avoid protease‑inhibitor interactions with tyrosine‑kinase inhibitors; screen for opportunistic infections before immunotherapy.

Low‑resource settings: rely on ultrasound and AFP for surveillance; use surgical resection or percutaneous ethanol injection when ablation equipment unavailable; prioritize affordable systemic agents (e.g., sorafenib) and enrol in regional trials.

sections.p: Sample questions covering bedside, investigations, management and special circumstances.
b: 1. Which bedside sign distinguishes ascites from pleural effusion and how is it performed?
2. How does the serum‑ascites albumin gradient differentiate portal hypertension‑related ascites from malignant ascites?
3. A patient with BCLC stage B disease progresses after two TACE cycles. What is the next evidence‑based systemic option?

7. How does chronic HBV integrate into host DNA to promote carcinogenesis?
8. A HIV‑positive man on efavirenz develops HCC and is started on sorafenib. What interaction should you monitor?
9. Describe the management steps for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis in an HCC patient.
10. For a pregnant woman at 12 weeks gestation with a 2.5 cm HCC, outline the safest diagnostic and therapeutic plan.

facts: AFP >400 ng/mL strongly supports HCC but is not required for diagnosis.
BCLC stage 0: single lesion ≤2 cm, Child‑Pugh A, ECOG 0.
BCLC stage A: single ≤5 cm or up to 3 lesions ≤3 cm, Child‑Pugh A‑B, ECOG 0‑1.
Child‑Pugh points: Bilirubin ≤2 mg/dL = 1 point, 2‑3 mg/dL = 2, >3 mg/dL = 3; INR ≤1.7 = 1, 1.71‑2.3 = 2, >2.3 = 3; Albumin ≥3.5 g/dL = 1, 2.8‑3.4 = 2, <2.8 = 3.
MELD score ≥15 generally indicates transplant referral.
Aflatoxin B1 is produced by Aspergillus flavus and Aspergillus parasiticus.
HBV chronicity in adults ≈5‑10%; HCV chronicity ≈75‑85%.
First‑line systemic options for advanced HCC: atezolizumab + bevacizumab, or durvalumab + tremelimumab, or sorafenib/lenvatinib where immunotherapy unavailable.
Hepatorenal syndrome: serum creatinine ≥1.5 mg/dL, no improvement after diuretics, absence of shock or nephrotoxic drugs, and urine sodium <10 mmol/L.
SAAG ≥1.1 g/dL indicates portal hypertension‑related ascites; <1.1 g/dL suggests peritoneal disease or infection.

mnemonics.t: Ascites, Bleeding, Cancer (HCC), Dysphagia (esophageal varices), Encephalopathy – key complications to screen for in cirrhosis.

vivas.q: What are the three components of the BCLC staging system?
vivas.a: Tumour burden, liver function (Child‑Pugh), and performance status (ECOG).

vivas.q: How do you differentiate HCC from liver metastases on contrast‑enhanced CT?
vivas.a: HCC shows arterial phase hyperenhancement with rapid washout in portal venous phase; metastases usually lack washout and may be rim‑enhancing.

vivas.q: Why is AFP alone insufficient for HCC surveillance?
vivas.a: AFP has low sensitivity for early tumours and can be elevated in chronic hepatitis; imaging is required for confirmation.

vivas.q: A patient with chronic HCV achieves SVR after DAAs. Why does HCC risk persist?
vivas.a: Cirrhotic architecture and residual dysplastic nodules remain; viral eradication does not reverse established fibrosis.

vivas.q: Which fungal genus produces aflatoxin B1 implicated in HCC?
Name the chemical carcinogen from mouldy grains that most commonly induces HCC.
What is the normal cellular function of p53 that is lost in many HCCs?
vivas.a: p53 induces cell‑cycle arrest and apoptosis in response to DNA damage, preventing malignant transformation.

vivas.q: Which serum tumour marker is classically associated with HCC and germ‑cell tumours?
How does HBV promote oncogenesis beyond chronic inflammation?
vivas.a: HBV DNA integrates into host genome, producing HBx protein that disrupts tumour‑suppressor pathways.

vivas.q: In HBV‑related HCC, which statement best describes liver pathology risk?
vivas.a: HCC can arise in non‑cirrhotic HBV liver, but risk rises sharply with cirrhosis.

vivas.q: Compare adult HBV and HCV chronicity rates and their HCC association.
vivas.a: HBV: ~5‑10% chronic in adults, high HCC risk even without cirrhosis; HCV: ~75‑85% chronic, HCC risk mainly after cirrhosis develops.

vivas.q: Interpret HBsAg‑, anti‑HBs‑, anti‑HBc IgM‑positive serology.
vivas.a: Acute hepatitis B infection (window period) – core IgM indicates recent infection.

vivas.q: What bedside examination steps confirm ascites and what cannot be determined at the bedside?
vivas.a: Inspect for distension, percuss flanks for dullness, perform shifting dullness and fluid thrill; bedside cannot grade volume precisely or differentiate malignant vs transudate.

vivas.q: When is a liver biopsy indicated in suspected HCC?
vivas.a: When imaging is atypical (no classic arterial washout) and AFP is non‑diagnostic; also before systemic therapy if histology will change management.

vivas.q: Why is atezolizumab + bevacizumab not universally first‑line in low‑resource settings?
vivas.a: Cost and need for safe administration of anti‑VEGF (risk of bleeding) limit its availability; sorafenib or lenvatinib may be used instead.

mcqs.q: A 58‑year‑old man with HBV cirrhosis presents with a 3‑cm liver lesion on ultrasound. AFP is 450 ng/mL. According to BCLC, his stage is:
mcqs.e: Single ≤5 cm lesion with Child‑Pugh A/B and ECOG 0‑1 fits BCLC stage A.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step for a patient with compensated cirrhosis (Child‑Pugh A) and a solitary 1.5‑cm lesion showing arterial enhancement and portal washout?
o: Observe with repeat imaging in 6 months
mcqs.e: Lesions ≤2 cm with typical imaging are curable by ablative therapy; surgery reserved for larger or multiple lesions.

mcqs.q: A 45‑year‑old woman with NAFLD cirrhosis has ascites. SAAG is 1.3 g/dL. The most likely cause is:
mcqs.e: SAAG ≥1.1 g/dL indicates portal hypertension‑related ascites.

mcqs.q: Which systemic therapy combination is contraindicated in a patient with untreated esophageal varices?
mcqs.e: Bevacizumab (anti‑VEGF) increases bleeding risk in varices.

mcqs.q: In a resource‑limited hospital lacking CT, what is the best surveillance strategy for a cirrhotic patient?
mcqs.e: Ultrasound every 6 months is the recommended low‑cost surveillance method.

mcqs.q: A patient with HCC and Child‑Pugh C liver disease is most appropriately managed with:
mcqs.e: Child‑Pugh C patients are generally unsuitable for TACE or systemic therapy; focus on palliation.

cases.v: A 62‑year‑old man with known HBV cirrhosis (Child‑Pugh B) presents with right‑upper‑quadrant pain, weight loss, and a 4‑cm lesion on triphasic CT showing arterial hyperenhancement and washout. AFP is 520 ng/mL.

qs.a: Stage B (intermediate) – multiple or single lesion >3 cm with Child‑Pugh B.

qs.q: What is the first‑line treatment option in a low‑resource setting?
qs.a: Transarterial chemoembolisation (TACE) if liver function permits; otherwise consider systemic sorafenib.

qs.q: Which complication should be screened for before therapy?
qs.a: Esophageal varices (risk of bleeding with anti‑VEGF agents) and hepatic encephalopathy; perform endoscopy and assess mental status.

cases.v: A 45‑year‑old woman with HCV‑related cirrhosis (Child‑Pugh A) is found on surveillance ultrasound to have a 1.8‑cm nodule with typical HCC imaging features. AFP is 120 ng/mL.

qs.q: What curative option is most appropriate?
qs.a: Radiofrequency ablation, as lesion ≤2 cm with preserved liver function.
Ultrasound and AFP every 3‑6 months for the first 2 years, then every 6‑12 months.

qs.q: If the patient later develops ascites, how do you differentiate portal‑hypertensive from malignant ascites?
qs.a: Calculate SAAG; ≥1.1 g/dL suggests portal hypertension, <1.1 g/dL suggests malignant or infectious cause.

mistakes: Assuming AFP >400 ng/mL is required for HCC diagnosis; imaging can confirm without AFP.
Confusing BCLC stage 0 and stage A lesion size limits; stage A includes lesions up to 5 cm.
Using Child‑Pugh bilirubin >2 mg/dL as a universal cut‑off; exact point thresholds differ for each class.
Prescribing atezolizumab + bevacizumab in patients with untreated varices without endoscopic control.
Relying on a single AFP measurement; serial trends are more informative.
Neglecting to assess for hepatorenal syndrome when creatinine rises; HRS has specific diagnostic criteria.
Over‑interpreting a negative ultrasound as ruling out HCC; small lesions may be missed, repeat imaging is needed.
Failing to consider aflatoxin exposure in patients from tropical regions with no viral risk factors.
exam: What are the three components of the BCLC staging system? — Tumour burden, liver function (Child‑Pugh), and performance status (ECOG).

How do you differentiate HCC from liver metastases on contrast‑enhanced CT? — HCC shows arterial phase hyperenhancement with rapid washout in portal venous phase; metastases usually lack washout and may be rim‑enhancing.
Why is AFP alone insufficient for HCC surveillance? — AFP has low sensitivity for early tumours and can be elevated in chronic hepatitis; imaging is required for confirmation.

A patient with chronic HCV achieves SVR after DAAs. Why does HCC risk persist? — Cirrhotic architecture and residual dysplastic nodules remain; viral eradication does not reverse established fibrosis.
Which fungal genus produces aflatoxin B1 implicated in HCC? — Aspergillus (A. flavus and A. parasiticus).
Name the chemical carcinogen from mouldy grains that most commonly induces HCC. — Aflatoxin B1.
What is the normal cellular function of p53 that is lost in many HCCs? — p53 induces cell‑cycle arrest and apoptosis in response to DNA damage, preventing malignant transformation.
Which serum tumour marker is classically associated with HCC and germ‑cell tumours? — Alpha‑fetoprotein (AFP).
How does HBV promote oncogenesis beyond chronic inflammation? — HBV DNA integrates into host genome, producing HBx protein that disrupts tumour‑suppressor pathways.
In HBV‑related HCC, which statement best describes liver pathology risk? — HCC can arise in non‑cirrhotic HBV liver, but risk rises sharply with cirrhosis.

Compare adult HBV and HCV chronicity rates and their HCC association. — HBV: ~5‑10% chronic in adults, high HCC risk even without cirrhosis; HCV: ~75‑85% chronic, HCC risk mainly after cirrhosis develops.
Interpret HBsAg‑, anti‑HBs‑, anti‑HBc IgM‑positive serology. — Acute hepatitis B infection (window period) – core IgM indicates recent infection.

What bedside examination steps confirm ascites and what cannot be determined at the bedside? — Inspect for distension, percuss flanks for dullness, perform shifting dullness and fluid thrill; bedside cannot grade volume precisely or differentiate malignant vs transudate.

When is a liver biopsy indicated in suspected HCC? — When imaging is atypical (no classic arterial washout) and AFP is non‑diagnostic; also before systemic therapy if histology will change management.
